title: Intel's Optane Died Because 3D NAND Was Too Cheap, Not Because the Tech Was Bad
dek: Phase-change memory was worked on from 1970 to 2022, and every time it was squeezed out by cheaper flash. 3D XPoint was stuck between NAND and DRAM, worse than both, and in the end even Intel gave up on it.
why: A complete history of a storage technology's failure, from RMM in 1970 to Optane's shutdown in 2022. Medium information density; the back half on data-center deployment and Micron's exit is the most valuable part.
who: Engineers and investors watching memory chips, data-center hardware and semiconductor industry history, especially anyone who wants to understand why a new technology gets squeezed out by a cheaper old one.
skip: The first minute of technical background can be fast-forwarded; jump straight to the phase-change storage mechanism at 3:07.

points.h: The physics of phase-change storage is what makes it slow
points.body: Phase-change storage stores data by switching a material between a crystalline and an amorphous state: the crystalline state has low resistance, the amorphous state high resistance, and the two differ by three to four orders of magnitude. Melting the material and quenching it into the amorphous state is called RESET; the reverse is called SET. SET either melts the material into a liquid and then cools it slowly so it crystallizes, or heats it to a temperature high enough to convert it directly to crystal without melting. The author points out that SET is often the speed bottleneck for PCM. This physical mechanism has not changed since Stanford Ovshinsky discovered the phase-change behavior of chalcogenide compounds in the 1960s.

points.h: Intel built phase-change memory in 1970, then forgot
points.body: In 1970, RG Neale and DL Nelson of Energy Conversion Devices and Intel's Gordon Moore published an article in Electronics magazine announcing "Read-Mostly Memory," positioned between RAM and ROM, for storing data that programs read often but rarely change. Each cell was a silicon diode plus a layer of phase-change material; Intel supplied the silicon substrate, ECD supplied the material. But in 1970 the minimum feature size was only 10 microns, power consumption was high, SET took milliseconds, and endurance was low. DRAM capacity was growing, EPROM arrived, and RMM disappeared. Years later someone asked the 79-year-old Moore about the article, and he said he had no memory of it at all.

points.h: Numonyx treated PCM as its only shot at a comeback
points.body: The rise of NAND sent NOR flash into a long decline, and in 2007 global NOR sales fell 9% year over year. Intel merged its NOR business with STMicroelectronics' flash business, forming the Swiss company Numonyx in 2008, with an investment from Francisco Partners and a bank loan. NOR had none of NAND's growth prospects, so Numonyx could only bet on PCM — PCM combined NOR's fast random reads with NAND's high-capacity storage, and in theory could replace both. In February 2008 Intel announced delivery of its first PCM prototype, Alverstone, at 128 megabit and 90 nanometers.

points.h: Mobile PCM was wiped out in one wave by 3D NAND
points.body: PCM's entry strategy was to attack the mobile market, replacing the NOR flash that stores boot code while also storing data. In 2009 Samsung announced a 512 megabit PRAM at 60 nanometers, saying that paired with DRAM it could save more than 20% of power. Micron acquired Numonyx in 2010 for about $1.2 billion in stock, and in July 2012 finally shipped 1 gigabit PCM at 45 nanometers, which Nokia put into its Asha feature phones. But in August 2013 Samsung announced mass production of 24-layer 3D NAND, and 3D NAND then set off the steepest cost-decline curve in semiconductor history, and mobile PCM's most compelling rationale was gone. In January 2014 Micron announced it was pulling out of mobile PCM.

points.h: Intel and Micron were split on Optane's positioning from the start
points.body: In July 2018 Intel and Micron agreed to a friendly split, each going its own way after completing joint development of second-generation 3D XPoint. The disagreement was over product direction: Intel initially aimed Optane SSDs at consumer PCs and laptops, hoping volume would dilute wafer costs; Micron wanted to go straight into the data center. Jon Carter hinted back in 2016 that consumer systems did not really need 3D XPoint's low latency, non-volatility and endurance, or at least not enough to pay four to five times the price of NAND for them. In October 2018 Micron announced it would pay $1.5 billion to buy Intel's half of the IM Flash plant in Utah, and Intel switched to producing it itself.

points.h: Putting Optane into the data center meant redoing motherboards and software
points.body: In April 2019 the first DIMM-form-factor Optane DC Persistent Memory went on sale, four years after 3D XPoint was announced, and it required matching Xeon processors, chipsets and motherboards. It had two modes: Memory Mode pooled Optane and DRAM into a single volatile memory pool, worked out of the box, but its value depended on DRAM price swings; App Direct Mode was the mode that was truly valuable, letting software write persistent data into Optane so it was still there after a reboot. Restarting an Oracle or SAP database usually takes more than an hour to reload data from SSDs or hard drives, and Optane could eliminate that. One imprecise but directionally useful test showed a 12.5x improvement. But App Direct Mode required programmers to rethink data consistency.

points.h: Only 40% of 582 proofs of concept used the mode that actually mattered
points.body: In 2020 Intel updated Optane adoption, saying there were 582 proofs of concept in the pipeline, with SAP HANA and Oracle Exadata the main users and the rest mostly in high-performance computing, infrastructure and some AI analytics. But only 40% used the more valuable App Direct Mode. Intel said it believed the industry would eventually adopt that mode, but it might take years. In the same period Intel announced the sale of its 3D NAND business to SK hynix for $9 billion, with Optane not part of the deal — seemingly an endorsement, but it also let people infer that Optane's implied loss in 2020 was more than $500 million.

points.h: After Micron left, Optane had only a single supplier
points.body: In March 2021 Micron announced it was immediately stopping 3D XPoint development, saying the Utah plant had long suffered from underutilization and dragged $400 million a year off the company, and the plant was later sold to Texas Instruments. Micron attributed the decision to 3D NAND prices continuing to fall, and to the hard changes data centers and applications would have to make to take full advantage of the product. Micron pivoted to betting on the open-standard interface CXL, because machine-learning systems made Micron realize that not just CPUs needed more memory — GPUs and AI accelerator ASICs did too. Micron's public exit severely weakened Optane: customers could rely only on Intel as a single source, and Optane was proprietary technology. In July 2022 Intel quietly announced on its earnings call that it was shutting down the Optane business.

terms.def: A non-volatile memory technology jointly announced by Intel and Micron in 2015, later turned into Optane and QuantX respectively.
A non-volatile memory that stores data using the resistance difference between a material's crystalline and amorphous states.
A memory category between hard drives and solid-state storage, combining non-volatility with access speeds close to DRAM.
Optane's persistent memory mode, in which software can write persistent data directly to the Optane module.
An open-standard interface that connects compute, memory and storage systems into pools that can be allocated on demand.
